title: Autonomous Penetration Testing and Cyber Defense with LLM Agents: A Self-Play Reinforcement Learning Arena
content: Autonomous penetration testing and autonomous defense are attractive applications of large language model (LLM) agents, but improving such agents with reinforcement learning requires an environment in which attacks are legal, reproducible, and scored without a human or a reward model in the loop. An exploratory policy can not be allowed to damage third-party systems, a reward measured on one rollout must remain comparable on the next rollout even though the policy changed, and a learned reward model or an LLM judge would place a second, possibly reward-hackable, model inside the training loop. To solve this problem, we created RL-CyberBench, a self-play arena that runs entirely inside Docker and containerlab. One attacker LLM agent and one defender LLM agent share an identical Kali Linux toolbelt, and they alternately attack and harden a reverse-proxy firewall that protects Go web servers holding a per-round randomized secret, while innocent Go clients must keep retrieving the secret through the firewall. Every LLM input, output, and tool call is logged, IP addresses and secrets are re-randomized every round, and a deterministic pure-Python judge parses JSON artifacts against fixed scoring tables, so no LLM judge and no learned reward model are involved. The repository implements five stages: a toolbelt of two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and five agent skills, an arena with a 25-round inference collection, aggregation into Unsloth supervised fine-tuning files, supervised fine-tuning of Qwen3.8-27B with 4-bit quantized low-rank adaptation, and judge-backed group relative policy optimization that yields an attacker policy with weights different from the defender policy. Verification checks confirm that the trained weights differ from the initial weights and that the two policies diverge, and a FastAPI web interface monitors and controls both inference and training. The arena isolates every lab container from the internet and from the management network, and the seeded vulnerability is a disabled web application firewall (WAF) that the defender must repair. In the future, the same configuration-driven generator may deploy richer topologies without code changes.
